planting.note: Plant in a sunny, sharply-drained spot such as a rock garden edge or path where the citrus-caraway scent releases when the low mat of foliage is brushed.

directions: A sport of the classic caraway thyme, this cultivar layers orange citrus notes over the usual caraway fragrance. It forms a tight, low mat best suited to full sun and lean, fast-draining soil rather than rich garden loam. Use the leaves as a culinary caraway substitute or simply as a fragrant edging plant. Shear lightly after flowering to keep growth dense.

common_name: White Moss Thyme (Non-Fragrant Creeping Groundcover Thyme)

planting.note: Install in full sun between pavers or along paths, where the fast-spreading mat tolerates light foot traffic as a lawn alternative.

directions: Unlike most thymes, this white-flowered selection carries little to no fragrance, which makes it a candidate for areas that get brushed or walked on often. It spreads quickly into a dense evergreen mat topped with white summer blooms, so give it room or use it to fill gaps between stepping stones. It needs full sun and gritty, well-drained soil to avoid rot in wet winters. Light shearing after bloom keeps the mat tidy.

planting.note: Give this vine a trellis or fence in full sun to light shade; because the pure-white flowers set very little seed, propagate new plants from softwood cuttings instead.

directions: This cultivar arose as a naturally occurring white-flowered sport of the native maypop passionflower, and it blooms heavily but almost never sets viable seed. Because of that, it must be propagated from cuttings rather than seed, which keeps it less common than the typical lavender-flowered species. The vine dies back to its hardy root system each winter and regrows vigorously in spring, so give it a sturdy trellis and full sun to part shade. It is valued both as a striking ornamental vine and for the same medicinal traditions associated with wild maypop.

common_name: Rober's Lemon Rose Geranium (Lemon-Rose Scented Geranium)

planting.note: Move outdoors only after frost danger passes and bring containers back inside before fall frost, since this is a tender perennial outside zones 8-11.

directions: This scented geranium's distinctive goosefoot-shaped leaves give off a strong lemon-rose fragrance and are reputed to contain more natural insect-repelling compounds than the common 'mosquito plant' geranium. It grows into a loose, sprawling shrub with occasional small pink flowers through summer. Grow it in full sun with well-drained soil and overwinter indoors in a bright window where winters are cold. Pinch growing tips regularly to keep the sprawling habit in check.

planting.note: Plant in poor, sharply-drained soil in full sun; it is a tender perennial that only occasionally survives winters as far north as Ohio.

directions: This low, mounding sub-shrub carries crinkled, grey-green leaves with a strong sweet aroma, even though the foliage tastes quite bitter. Rose-pink flower spikes appear above the foliage in season. It does best in lean, fast-draining soil rather than fertile garden beds, and its compact, woody habit makes it a popular subject for bonsai training. Treat it as tender outside of warm climates and take cuttings in fall as insurance against winter loss.

planting.note: Plant at a pond margin or in consistently moist soil in partial shade to full sun, though it will also tolerate average garden moisture once established.

directions: With slender, grass-like foliage and a true licorice scent and taste, this sweet flag selection is used fresh or dried in Thai cooking and brewed as a digestive tea. It thrives in boggy or pond-edge conditions but adapts reasonably well to normal garden moisture once its roots are established. Traditional use includes easing loss of appetite and mild gastric upset. Divide clumps in spring to propagate and keep the planting vigorous.

planting.note: Set out container plants after all frost danger has passed, spacing roughly 3 feet apart so the odor forms a continuous barrier around garden beds.

directions: This patented ornamental Plectranthus was bred specifically for its odor, which is disagreeable to cats and dogs but imperceptible or pleasant to most people, making it a living perimeter deterrent rather than a culinary herb. Its succulent leaves and lavender flowers add texture to a bed while the plant does double duty as a barrier. Because it is hardy only to zone 11 and up, gardeners in colder regions must grow it as a container plant or summer annual and bring it indoors before frost. Give it full sun and average water, and avoid propagating it yourself since the variety is under active patent protection.

planting.note: Start seed in containers in spring and keep seedlings potted through their first season, since young plants are prone to damping off and transplant best the following spring.

directions: A much less common relative of the familiar orange goji, this species produces small dark purple-black berries prized in Tibetan and Chinese herbal traditions for their unusually high antioxidant (OPC) content alongside vitamins A, C and E. It forms a wiry, drought-tolerant shrub best suited to dry, well-drained soils in full sun, and tolerates cold winters down to zone 4. Because seedlings are delicate, raise them in pots for the first year rather than direct-sowing into the garden. Once established it needs little supplemental water and is best treated like other xeric hedgerow shrubs.

planting.note: Plant alongside a male seabuckthorn at roughly one male per five females, since this is a female-only selection that will not set fruit without a nearby pollinator.

directions: Bred from the Russian 'Chuskaya' line, this female seabuckthorn cultivar ripens earlier than most other varieties and carries unusually large, juicy, palatable berries in late July into early August. It can be kept pruned to a manageable 5-foot hedge for easier harvesting rather than allowed to grow to its full size. Like all seabuckthorns it fixes nitrogen and thrives in poor, sandy, well-drained soil, tolerating drought once rooted in. Remember it is dioecious, so fruiting depends entirely on having a male plant nearby to pollinate it.

planting.note: Plant divisions in sun to part shade with generous airflow between plants, since crowded bee balm is prone to powdery mildew.

directions: This Monarda selection stands out among bee balms for its high geraniol content, which gives the lavender-colored flower heads and foliage a true rose-like fragrance rather than the typical minty-oregano scent of most bergamots. Steep the leaves fresh or dried for an aromatic tea, or dry the flowers for potpourri and sachets. Like other bee balms it draws bees, butterflies, and hummingbirds in large numbers once in bloom. Site it where air circulates freely and divide clumps every few years to maintain vigor and reduce mildew pressure.

planting.note: Sow in spring, late summer, or early fall into gritty, acidic, sharply drained soil; germination is easy compared to European Arnica montana.

directions: Tested by the Vienna Pharmacognostic Institute to match the medicinal action of true European Arnica montana, this North American species is prized by growers specifically because it germinates and establishes far more readily than its temperamental European cousin. Its yellow daisy-like flowerheads are harvested and infused into salves, creams, or gels used topically for bruises, sprains, and osteoarthritic joint pain — never taken internally. It performs best in cool climates with acidic, well-drained soil, making raised beds and rock gardens good fits. Keep soil consistently but lightly moist, since it is an alpine native that dislikes both drought and waterlogging.

planting.note: Direct-sow into lean, rocky, fast-draining soil in full sun; established plants resent being moved because of their deep taproot.

directions: Unlike its purple-flowered relative Dyer's Alkanet, this eastern Mediterranean species bears cheerful yellow forget-me-not-like flowers over a low mound of bristly grey-green foliage. Its long taproot, like other Alkanna species, contains red dye compounds that have traditionally colored oils and salves, though the flowers are its main garden draw. Give it a dry, rocky, full-sun site similar to its native limestone scree habitat, since wet winter soil quickly rots the root. Once established it is drought-tolerant and long-lived, needing little care beyond an occasional tidy-up of spent flower stems.

planting.note: Scarify or soak seed before sowing to break the hard coat, start indoors or in a nursery pot, and only move outdoors in frost-free zones once well rooted.

directions: This thorny, drought-adapted tree from Africa and South Asia is the traditional source of true gum arabic, the hardened resin exuded from wounds in its bark and used for centuries as a food thickener, binder, and in traditional medicine. It fixes nitrogen through root nodules and tolerates poor, saline, and arid soils that defeat most other trees. Give it full sun and a protected frost-free site, since it is reliably hardy only in warm zones. Established trees need very little irrigation and can be tapped for gum once mature.

planting.note: Grow in a shallow pot of gritty, fast-draining cactus mix and keep frost-free year-round, since this critically endangered dwarf aloe has no cold tolerance.

directions: Native to a tiny area of northern Somalia and classified as critically endangered in the wild, this charming dwarf aloe forms a tight rosette of silvery-green leaves marked with pale H-shaped spots and soft marginal teeth. Coral-pink flower spikes rise well above the foliage in spring. Grow it as a container specimen in bright light with some protection from the most intense midday sun, in a mineral, well-drained potting mix. Keep it strictly frost-free and water sparingly, letting the mix dry fully between waterings.

planting.note: Pot in a gritty, fast-draining succulent mix and keep frost-free; this endangered species is grown mainly as a collector container plant outside its native Sudan.

directions: Native to a small region of eastern Sudan and listed as endangered in its native range, this aloe forms a stemless rosette of broad, spiny-margined leaves topped by branched spikes of orange-red flowers. It is closely related to Aloe vera and has traditionally been used in similar topical and medicinal preparations. Grow it in full sun with sharply draining mineral soil, keeping it strictly frost-free since it has no cold hardiness. Allow the soil to dry completely between waterings to avoid root and crown rot.

planting.note: Grow in full sun in very well-drained soil or a large container; it eventually forms a tree-like rosette too large for small pots.

directions: This southern African aloe grows into a dramatic, multi-headed rosette of broad grey-green leaves on a short, thick stem, eventually reaching tree-like proportions. Its namesake bottle-brush flower spikes open in dense, upright clusters of orange-yellow blooms that are strongly attractive to sunbirds in its native range. It needs full sun and sharply draining, mineral soil to avoid rot, and is only reliably hardy outdoors in nearly frost-free zones. Container-grown plants should be moved to a bright, dry spot indoors wherever winter frost is a risk.

planting.note: Grow in a large container with a sturdy support for the sprawling, winged stems, and give it a very well-drained cactus mix in bright light.

directions: This sprawling, climbing cactus from Mexico produces one of the most spectacular night-blooming flowers of any cactus — a fragrant, foot-wide bloom with narrow outer petals that opens for a single night and closes by morning. Its thin, winged, blue-green stems scramble over rocks or other plants in habitat and need a trellis or support when grown in cultivation. Give it a bright spot with some protection from the harshest midday sun and a fast-draining cactus mix, watering moderately during active growth and much less in winter. It is grown almost entirely for its dramatic once-a-year flowering event rather than year-round ornamental appeal.

planting.note: Cold-stratify seed before sowing, grow on in a nursery pot for at least a year, and transplant to a permanent well-drained site with ample room for a large mature tree.

directions: Native to mountain forests of the western United States, this long-lived conifer forms a dense, narrow, pyramidal crown of aromatic, scale-like foliage that releases a spicy incense scent when crushed — the same wood traditionally used for pencils and cedar closet linings. It tolerates a wide range of soils, from rocky mountain slopes to heavier garden loam, and once established is notably drought-tolerant for a conifer. Give young trees full sun and consistent moisture to establish, after which they need little supplemental water. Plan for its eventual large size, since mature specimens can exceed 100 feet, and keep it well away from structures or power lines.
